results.verdict: Oasis describes the most thorough PayPal integration on paper (Orders v2, server-side capture with amount checks, idempotency, verified webhooks, Payouts royalties, refunds), but the live site reports paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, the agent page shows 'The agent isn't configured on this server', every proof number is a {{placeholder}}, only 9 tests back the testing claims, it isn't submitted to Devpost, and the store copies Polyfork's concept, copy and layout almost line for line, so a developer today can see a handsome storefront but cannot watch a single PayPal order get approved or captured.
fixes: Set the PayPal sandbox and Anthropic credentials on Render so /api/config returns paypalReady:true and agentReady:true. Then confirm the full path live: Buy now opens Smart Buttons, the buyer approves, the server captures and the licensed download unlocks. Prove the agent chat runs the same path from a brief.

Replace every {{placeholder}} with real sandbox evidence: order IDs, capture IDs, payout batch IDs for a fork-of-fork split showing 60/30/10 to three sandbox accounts, a webhook event log (CHECKOUT.ORDER.APPROVED, PAYMENT.CAPTURE.REFUNDED, PAYOUTS-ITEM), and the refund count. Delete any number you can't back. Then actually submit on Devpost.

Record a 2–3 minute demo that shows each step without cuts: Claude via `/mcp` calls create_order and returns the payer-action link, the human approves in PayPal's window, get_order captures and returns downloads, and the royalty payouts appear in the sandbox dashboard. This is the agentic-commerce story that beat the field at Dev Days (CrawlerPal), and it is currently invisible.

Back the claims with tests and a doc a developer can learn from. Add tests for the capture amount/currency mismatch that triggers an auto-refund, webhook signature verification, the capture-lock race, the 799-cent royalty split and the QuickJS memory-bomb kill. Publish a PAYPAL.md walkthrough of the order→approve→capture→webhook→payout code. Also differentiate the hero and asset pages from Polyfork, so the original pieces (Brand Mode and the human-approved agent order) lead instead of the borrowed concept.

results.verdict: Oasis has a well-designed payment architecture on paper (idempotency keys, a capture lock, amount-checked capture, verified webhooks, a QuickJS sandbox killed from outside) and a polished but closely Polyfork-derived storefront, yet the live deployment shows paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, the agent page says it isn't configured, every proof number is still a {{placeholder}}, the factory log contradicts the grader claims, and the entry isn't submitted, so none of the agentic-payment story is demonstrated end to end.
fixes: Make the core flow actually work live. Set the PayPal sandbox credentials and the Anthropic key on Render so /api/config reports paypalReady:true and agentReady:true. Then run and record one unbroken flow: brief, agent remixes, cart, PayPal order, human approval, server-side capture with amount check, licensed download, royalty payout. Link the video and give judges sandbox buyer credentials.

Replace every {{placeholder}} with real numbers pulled from logs and sandbox order IDs, then submit on Devpost. Reconcile the visible contradictions or remove the claims: factory v2 logged 1 build with 0 rejections against a claimed grader reject rate, and the catalogue shows 41 built-in assets against 43 assets plus 3 forks.

Back the robustness claims with tests. Nine tests can't cover what the writeup asserts. Add tests and CI for: duplicate capture racing across browser, return URL and webhook with the same PayPal-Request-Id; amount or currency mismatch triggering an auto-refund; webhook signature failure being rejected; the refund webhook revoking a licence; payout failure and retry; the cent-exact royalty split along a fork chain; and the sandbox escape and worker-kill cases.

Harden agent-initiated payments beyond 'a human approves'. Enforce the brief's budget cap on the server before create_order. Rate-limit and attribute the unauthenticated MCP create_order calls. Show the requesting agent and the itemised remix in the order description. Log an audit trail per order. Also give the UI an identity that doesn't mirror Polyfork's hero copy and layout line for line.

results.verdict: Oasis is a polished storefront that knowingly copies Polyfork's model, but its PayPal pitch is not proven: the live server reports paypalReady:false and agentReady:false, the agent page shows 'The agent isn't configured on this server', every proof number is still a {{placeholder}}, only 9 tests exist and 1 factory-v2 build is logged, and the entry is unsubmitted, so today it is claims plus nice screenshots.
fixes: Make the core loop work on the live URL: configure PayPal sandbox credentials and the Claude agent. Then record an unedited video that goes from brief to branded kit to the PayPal approval window to capture to licensed download, plus one fork-of-fork Payouts split. The agent-creates-order, human-approves flow is your only real differentiator from Polyfork, and right now a judge cannot see it.

Replace every {{placeholder}} with real, verifiable numbers: orders captured, payouts, refunds, assets, knobs and grader rejection rate. Link them to /api/stats or sandbox transaction IDs. Delete or soften any claim you can't back, such as broad test coverage when only 9 tests exist, or factory scale when only 1 v2 build is logged.

Get outside evidence of demand before the deadline: a handful of real users or external MCP keys making calls, a few paid (even sandbox-to-live) licences, and one creator whose fork earned a royalty. Polyfork wins on 54 paying customers and $4,428, while you have zero users.

Submit on Devpost and reframe the story around PayPal, not Polyfork. Lead with the agentic-commerce primitive: server-priced orders, the capture lock, webhook recovery, auto-refund on amount mismatch, and lineage royalties via Payouts. Show the approval UI, and keep the 'Polyfork for 2D' framing to one line.

results.verdict: Oasis has a beautifully crafted, Polyfork-shaped storefront and a sharp agent-proposes/human-approves PayPal idea, but the live site has PayPal and the agent switched off (paypalReady:false, agentReady:false, 'The agent isn't configured on this server'), the write-up is still full of {{placeholders}}, and it isn't submitted, so nothing that would make it a PayPal winner is proven.
fixes: Make the core loop work on the live URL. Configure the PayPal sandbox credentials and the Anthropic key on Render so /api/config reports paypalReady:true and agentReady:true. Then run real briefs through agent, remix, PayPal approval, capture and licensed download, and publish a sandbox buyer login so judges can complete a checkout themselves.

Replace every {{placeholder}} with numbers you can show, and reconcile what you have against what you claim. Currently there are 41 built-in vs 43 assets, 9 tests, and 1 factory-v2 build. Link captured order IDs and payout batch IDs, or cut any claim (royalty payouts, refunds, grader reject rate, sandbox-escape tests) you can't back up today.

Record a 2–3 minute video and submit to Devpost. Show Brand Mode recolouring the catalogue, then the agent building the Tidepool kit and rejecting its own render. Show PayPal's approval window, the capture, and the 60/30/10 payout split landing for a fork-of-a-fork. Finish with an external Claude client using /mcp from create_order to get_order.

Make the asset store look like its own product rather than a Polyfork re-skin, and make the agent page useful even when the agent is unavailable. The headline, 'Exports to' strip, 'How it works' and 'Use it' layout map nearly one-to-one onto Polyfork. Lead the hero with the brand-plus-PayPal-approval story instead. Replace the empty agent pane with a replayable recorded session showing the renders, the cart and the PayPal order.
